In a recent development, apple confirmed a newly introduced study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The organization is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance.

Sources indicate that the app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later.

Study participants can use the app to ask health-related questions and receive easily understandable responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources. The app relies on text-based prompts, and while dictation is an option using the iOS keyboard, the app isn’t integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence.

It has been revealed that during enrolment, participants are given the option to share Apple HealthKit data, like their activity, sleep, or clinical lab results, so responses will include more context about their own personal health. But privacy is a priority, and Apple says it has taken measures to ensure customers’ information remains confidential and the data collected won’t be used to train AI models. The aim is to improve the design and functionality of AI-powered health tools so they can deliver relevant health information that’s easier for users to understand and act on.

It has been revealed that “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” said Sumbul Desai, MD, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

#383. Industry News: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess

Industry News: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
  • But just as he’s leaving, the manufacturer has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck.
  • In a recent development, “Everything sold today was designed two-to-three years ago,” states the CEO of a large AI tech giant, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving, the manufacturer has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

In a recent development, “Everything sold today was designed two-to-three years ago,” states the CEO of a large AI tech giant, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

Industry observers note that nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

In a recent development, massive US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a organization that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more notable. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Grok, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorehead remarked, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

According to recent reports, in 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI, China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the tech giant’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Recent findings suggest that huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

Sources indicate that huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Sources indicate that most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Moorhead indicates the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave.“They have access to AI too,” he notes.

Recent findings suggest that but Moorhead notes the way AI models can now promptly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he notes. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the manufacturer’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amid the Jensen Huang fallout, Maria Cantwell accuses Howard Lutnick of giving away ‘America’s technology advantage in AI.’﻿.

Amid the Jensen Huang fallout, Maria Cantwell accuses Howard Lutnick of giving away ‘America’s technology advantage in AI.’﻿.

Washington Senator Maria Cantwell, one of the top Democrats on the Senate commerce committee, has taken fire at the Department of Commerce (DOC) under Secretary Howard Lutnick for neglecting to enforce protections intended to keep Nvidia’s AI chips away from China. In a letter to Lutnick on Sunday, Cantwell remarked the DOC has “undermined America’s national security,” and that its failures “help give away America’s technology advantage in AI.”.

“Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology.”.

In her letter, Cantwell specifically calls out instances when the DOC reportedly didn’t heed warnings from White House and intelligence officials to restrict Megaspeed’s access to AI chips, prior to allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a then-Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese spy. Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries.

The DOC is also accused of “putting business interests ahead of national security,” with Cantwell noting that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Lutnick and now steered by his sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of Lutnick’s nomination for Commerce Secretary.

According to recent reports, the letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. While Congress is looking to bolster export restrictions around AI chips, The Wall Street Journal reports that Lutnick is instead expected to unveil a new initiative that will designate Nvidia — along with companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, and Microsoft — as an AI “national champion.” The designation reportedly aims to help these companies expand overseas and compete with Chinese technology firms by granting them expedited export licence approvals.

“America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls,” Cantwell said, closing her letter. “The Administration must account for its failure to enforce these protections and take immediate action to prevent America’s most sensitive technology from strengthening our adversaries.”.

#379. Why Dispatch's creators mentioned no to '10,000 endings'

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1221 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq

Why Dispatch's creators mentioned no to '10,000 endings'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every interactive story faces the same temptation: give the player more.
  • It has been revealed that as the breakout indie game celebrates its one-year anniversary with the Dispatch Deluxe Edition, which lets you play the storyboard art, I caught up with the team.
  • AdHoc starts with the belief that most developers get the equation backwards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every interactive story faces the same temptation: give the player more. More branches, more endings, more ways to bend the script until it snaps. Dispatch, AdHoc Studio's episodic superhero workplace comedy, went the other way. It stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, who now sends a team of reformed villains out on call-outs.

It has been revealed that as the breakout indie game celebrates its one-year anniversary with the Dispatch Deluxe Edition, which lets you play the storyboard art, I caught up with the team. We've heard how Four video tracks and a doughnut shop got it started and how AdHoc made Dispatch feel like an animated TV series, so now I want to know how a choice-driven game gets that far by holding choices back. We put the question to AdHoc co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors.

AdHoc starts with the belief that most developers get the equation backwards. "When folks set out to make an interactive narrative game, they incorrectly assume that it's all about the branching narrative that makes it exciting," Herman says. "We believe it's about the quality of that narrative at the core, and then you have to branch that quality narrative.".

Recent findings suggest that that's easy to say and hard to do, he admits, and harder still when you have to write multiple good stories at once, which is what the team signed up for. So the development team works from the story's spine and its characters, then figure out what choice space could believably exist alongside them.

In a recent development, robert Robertson arrives with a backstory and a personality, so options that betray him are off the table. Herman sees that as a gift: it "eliminates blue sky" and lets the team concentrate on a believable character. It's also why he's wary when people ask for thousands of endings. Would 10,000 of them really be as compelling as a six or seven that the team has made as satisfying as possible?

In a recent development, lenart describes the whole process as "almost an exercise in restraint at times". Picture 10 developers in a room discussing a scene where a character is aggressive towards you. A couple of them will say they wish you could just punch him. "The thing we have to filter that through is, 'Would Robert conceivably punch him in this situation?'" notes Lenart. "A lot of times the answer is no.".

Industry observers note that it isn't a flat ban. If everyone agrees that punching him would be thrilling but there's no motivation for it, Herman says the conversation becomes how to make it a viable choice. Lenart says you go back into the scene and the story and set it up "so that that choice feels like it's a payoff to something that exists".

Sources indicate that skip that groundwork and the cost is steep. "The more you do that, the more you start diluting your character and then they kind of become a little bit faceless," Lenart warns. Herman puts it more bluntly: the story starts to feel like "a narrative toy" and less like one with believable characters.

So how do you make a choice feel weighty without animating an entirely newly introduced story? Lenart claims, "A lot of the magic in these types of games is the story that people are telling in their heads". The most effective choices, he says, are the ones where "you're affecting how another character in the story thinks about you".

Recent findings suggest that treat someone a certain way in front of the group, and players will assume that character's later behaviour is motivated by it. Every glance in a later scene gets read as payback for what you mentioned earlier, which Lenart compares to real life. AdHoc builds on that expectation on purpose.

Recent findings suggest that herman calls it "the grease between the major cogs of choices". Players carry a decision forward for an hour or so, until the grease runs out and they need an injection of upcoming stuff. If a scene doesn't land that way, he says, "it's probably because something's broken". Contrivance, or a sense of being guided, are the signs to go back and fix.

There's a hard budget reason for the discipline too. "It's also just so expensive to do it the way we're doing it," says Herman, with a vision for cinematic quality and animation that makes 30 different endings impossible.

Lenart gives an example of a branch the team could have offered. Imagine letting players choose at the start whether Robert works as a dispatcher or makes a upcoming suit and heads off to be a hero in another city. It sounds great on a flowchart, but "you'd end up animating an entirely different game", with two separate stories, and Robert's arc would stop being about redemption.

According to recent reports, herman is generous about other approaches. He points to Slay the Princess, The Stanley Parable, and Detroit: Become Human as games where their branchiness and reactivity are major selling points. "Interactive narrative games are not one thing," he indicates. "The beauty of the medium is that everyone finds ways to express it in different ways.".

Recent findings suggest that where does the line fall between what the player controls and what stays with the writers and developers? Lenart states it comes down to how much agency AdHoc is willing to hand over in order to tell a story it believes in. The more it gives up, the greater the risk of versions that aren't great. "Our goal was always to make it so that any path you play through is compelling and satisfying.".

Sources indicate that there's a cost, and AdHoc accepts it. Herman says some players will end up on a path that isn't their preference, and with stories it gets personal: "this isn't how I wanted it to go.".

Lenart has seen the other side of the argument. On earlier games, multiple endings were mandated as a studio priority, and the takeaway was that "some of them worked". Some people had good playthroughs, others got endings they weren't satisfied with, and some were upset they didn't get the endings their friends did.

He doesn't count loose ends as a failure, either. "Not every story or movie you watch ends with you thinking everything is perfect and wrapped up," he notes, and the threads people talk about afterwards are part of the experience. But "it can get out of hand if you don't keep it under control".

#378. Industry News: The Best Smart Bird Feeders for Backyard Birding (2026)

📅 19 Jul 2024 • ⏱️ 31m • 📚 Deep Dive (6210 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED

Industry News: The Best Smart Bird Feeders for Backyard Birding (2026)

📅 19 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one.
  • To answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints.
  • Recent findings suggest that updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a new Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one. The best smart bird feeders are easily recognizable with their clear housing, cameras, and solar panels. Perhaps a friend or family member has sent you a photo or video of a bright goldfinch or a handsome woodpecker (guilty). But are these feeders really worth their $100-plus price tag? Are they durable? And what about the squirrel problem?

To answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints. I’ve explored the apps and notification settings, examined the photo and video quality, noted which features are hidden behind a subscription paywall, and used Cornell Lab’s All About Birds—as well as Google Lens and my own expertise—to verify the accuracy of AI identifications. The recommendations below are what I would buy with my own money, having tested dozens of brands and models for a minimum of four weeks each.

Recent findings suggest that updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a new Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID. I've also removed a couple of discontinued feeders and updated links and prices.

It has been revealed that this cheery blue- or yellow-roofed feeder, from security manufacturer Netvue, was the first smart feeder WIRED tested, back in 2022, when it earned a 6/10 rating due to its high price and wonky AI. Both metrics have improved dramatically since then—Birdfy's app is now the second-most user-friendly on the market, behind only Birdbuddy's, and this feeder is often on sale for around $130. Its AI identification, which is decent, used to be paywalled but is now free with every tier of feeder.

Recent findings suggest that the 1080p/2K camera isn't the best quality you'll find, but it does have one of the widest viewing angles of any smart feeder, at 155 degrees, so you're more likely to get full bird shots, as opposed to just heads and butts. The plastic housing (available in blue or yellow) also makes this feeder durable and easy to clean, and the 50-ounce seed reservoir is super easy to fill with its convenient flip-up top. Not all bundles come with a solar panel, but you can buy one separately. Unlike with other feeders, the solar panel is not built in and needs to be mounted and connected separately with the included 9.8-foot charging cable.

It's not the fanciest feeder on the market, nor the one with the best camera, but I've never had a problem with the two models I've been rotating in and out throughout the years, and the reliability and price point make it the best bet for most backyard birders.

Target (Solar + Extended Perch).

Birdbuddy's brand-newly introduced Nook model is a lot of bird feeder for the price; it won our recent head-to-head test of sub-$100 smart feeders. The base $99 model doesn't come with a solar roof or extended perch, as seen in the photo above, but you will get a 2K HDR camera that can shoot vertically or horizontally (it pops in and out via a magnet), as well as the same sturdy, high-quality construction as Birdbuddy's pricier Home model. The seed capacity isn't the greatest at 0.9 liters, but the app is easy to use and can even identify birds nearby that don't land on the feeder, so long as its excellent onboard microphone hears their sounds.

Sources indicate that birdbuddy's Achilles’ heel has always been its sensor, which is slow to wake up and regularly misses bird visits. The fresh Birdbuddy feeder supposedly has a faster wake-up time than previous models, and though it still lagged behind Birdfy's competing Rookie feeder in capturing all visits, the Nook's rate was substantially better than the Home's. It also has more mounting options, allowing for hanging in addition to wall and pole mounts (though the latter is a loose fit), and allows for no-cost manual AI ID of all visitors.

It has been revealed that camojojo's original Hibird feeder has long been a reliable model in my testing stable, one of the first to run on both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi bands, and last year saw the debut of an upgraded model, the Hibird Pro. The update has built-in solar panels, an option for pole-mounting, and supposedly improved AI identification, though it still frequently misidentifies even common birds in my West Coast backyard as East Coast species. The app is not as streamlined or user-friendly as Birdfy's or Birdbuddy's, but it's still easy enough to navigate, with options for changing video length (default is 10 seconds) or viewing in slo-mo. The default media type it saves is video, though this is 4K Ultra HD, and the images are—as expected—extremely sharp. Without a subscription, you can't search past videos by bird, and cloud storage is capped at 5 GB over 60 days; however, the feeder does come with a 128-GB SD card. You'll also get “smarter” chats with the app's AI Q&A function, “Dr. Bird,” and the ability to share across two devices with a subscription ($45 per year or $4 per month).

Industry observers note that I appreciate the generous 1.5-liter seed hopper, although this, combined with the solar panel and battery, makes it extremely heavy. When filled, it tips the scales at 5 pounds, meaning that if you do pole-mount it, you will need to use both included hose clamps and wrench them tightly. I also wouldn't attempt to mount it on anything unstable, like a wobbly fence. Other original Hibird features that made it to the Pro include the little handles on the assembly screws (so you won't need any assembly tools) and the chunky plastic body. The latter was subjected to a little bit of squirrel-chewing during my test, but it still held up well.

Sources indicate that the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 is one of the most thoughtfully designed feeders on the market. You don't have to take down the whole feeder when refilling, as the 1.5-liter dual-hopper plastic seed reservoir is removable from the body. The 8-megapixel photos and 4K HD video have much better quality than you'll find from most competitors, and the components come apart for easy cleaning. I also tested the original version, which features a separate solar panel, and my only complaint was that the panel stopped charging the camera after about six weeks. This version features a built-in solar roof, which did an excellent job keeping the feeder charged during its six-week-long test, even on cloudy days. The plastic body is extremely thick and sturdy, and unlike lighter-weight feeders like Birdfy's, it's designed to hold up in more extreme weather.

The app is easy to navigate, and the whole setup is functional without a Kiwibit Plus subscription ($90/year, purchasable online or through the Kiwibit app) but you'll be losing out on a lot of features, including 60-day storage and the ability to record up to three minutes of video if a bird is doing something interesting—a unique feature among smart feeders, and one I discovered that I love. (There's nothing more frustrating than having a video cut off right as a bird is about to do something funny.) This smart feeder costs a bit much for what it is, but if you know you like having a smart feeder, I think it's worth the investment. Note, however, that it only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, and the warranty is half the length you get from many competitors. I also tested Kiwibit's newer model, the Feeder 2 Pro, and while its camera does have an interesting auto-zoom lens, I didn't think it was worth the $120 premium over this model.

Birdbuddy is known for its user-friendliness and thoughtful app—its Pro Smart Hummingbird Feeder is no exception. The feeder is intuitive and easy to use, and you don't need a subscription to access fun features like AI identification, 5 MP photos, and 2K HD video with slo-mo. A subscription unlocks features like family sharing and a higher bit rate, but the feeder is perfectly functional without those. With the panel being built into the feeder's roof, there’s also no auxiliary solar panel to worry about. Pairing with your phone is a cinch, integrating it into the Birdbuddy app with other feeders is a snap, and even refilling it is no problem. Unlike other hummingbird feeders that have weirdly cavernous capacities and/or need to be filled upside down, the Birdbuddy’s bottom screws off and holds a reasonable 1.75 cups of liquid. This detail is important; as the Cornell Lab of Ornithology points out, the easier it is to clean a hummingbird feeder, the more likely you are to do it often and well.

Recent findings suggest that this feeder also comes with extra plastic flowers and a little brush for scrubbing them, and the app sends reminders when it's time to clean. You'll find fun, seasonal touches in the app, like the ability to send digital bird holiday cards with the photos your feeder captures, and a tool that superimposes hats, clothes, and various accessories on the birds, which is actually funnier than it sounds. However, as with the Birdbuddy seed feeders, the massive downside is that the feeder's sensor doesn’t always pick up every bird that visits. This can definitely be a bummer, particularly when you see something interesting out the window but it doesn’t show up in the app.

After experiencing connection issues with the Birdfy Polygon, I swapped it out for the newer Birdfy Nest Duo and have had no issues. The sleek, contemporary Duo is a fir box fitted with two cameras—one facing the hole and one tucked discreetly inside the feeder. That gives you a full-spectrum view of what's going on. Both cameras have night vision (the internal one is infrared). Like the Polygon, the Duo sports a remote for rebooting and recharging the camera (though the separate solar panel, which can be pole-mounted, has kept the cameras reliably charged), as well as different-size holes for different species, each with its own chew-proof predator guard.

Sources indicate that there's a metal grate with drainage holes that you can slot into grooves in the lower third of the Nest to make the cavity larger or smaller. The interested birds of my yard seemed very put off by the grate, so I covered it with a layer of craft mat moss, which was a success—a chickadee promptly moved in and laid seven eggs, all of which hatched. (I detail the experience in a separate review). For the first time, I was able to use the Birdfy app's ability to collect images from its nest boxes and string them together in a “story” that's shareable online. But I didn't find it especially useful or accurate. No matter, though, because the video captures have been a truly fascinating and educational experience, and I wish I could afford to buy the Duo for everyone I know.

So far, the Duo has been rained on a bunch and survived a couple of heat waves, but the wood finish and black paint are peeling and will need refinishing before I put them up for next season. (The feeder comes equipped with a thermometer and hygrometer to keep an eye on conditions. I recently had to zip-tie an umbrella to mine during a heat wave, which likely saved some fledglings' lives, though the lightweight construction and black-painted side and top probably contributed to the box overheating.).

I rarely expect (or get) compliments on my backyard smart feeders, but I have gotten many on this one, which has a distinctively modern look with natural wood (bamboo that's FSC-certified to be responsibly sourced) and a black-painted side and roof. It blends right into the landscape as opposed to providing a visual pop of plastic. (The pole and baffle shown in the photo above are not included.).

In a recent development, birdfy's user-friendly app presents 2K HD images and video with free lifetime AI ID, and it's easy to share photos and videos with others. There's a solar panel you can mount separately, but I didn't do this and was impressed that the camera ran for nearly two months on an indoor USB-C charge.

Wood obviously comes with a higher risk of chewing by squirrels and other rodents, but there are metal guards available (both Birdfy-brand and aftermarket) that fit over the seed. I followed the 5-7-9 rule for pole-mounting to avoid this problem, but I was totally shocked at how weathered my feeder got after two months. And this was in a Pacific Northwest dry summer—about as mild as it gets. The finish was completely peeling off, so I recommend adding an extra layer of urethane (this is what I use) before putting it out for the first time, especially now, heading into winter.

What to Look for When Buying a Smart Bird Feeder.

It has been revealed that the world of smart bird feeders is vast and can seem overwhelming, but there are some key features that will really make a difference in your user experience. I've tested dozens of feeders for years from many different brands, and this is what I think you should pay attention to when comparing models.

It has been revealed that subscription: Most, if not all, smart bird feeders require a subscription to access all features. That's in order to support the company's continued investment in user experience. There are few things more disappointing than giving or receiving a smart bird feeder as a gift, only to find out it's not actually usable without shelling out an additional $70 a year. Reputable companies will note subscription requirements up front, and some even offer models that have a lifetime subscription built in. Note that if a feeder costs less than a hundred bucks, odds are it will require a subscription to capture photos, whether it states so in the marketing materials or not. You will need to do your due diligence before buying.

Industry observers note that mounting options: If you live in an area with squirrels, your best bet is to pole-mount your bird feeder—especially a more expensive smart feeder, which often has cords that squirrels and other rodents like to chew. Not all feeders offer a pole-mounting option, though, which is another key detail to confirm before buying.

In a recent development, wi-Fi network: The vast majority of smart feeders only work on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi frequencies. If you only use 5 GHz, you will need to look for a feeder that specifically works with a shorter transmission range or has dual range, such as the Camojojo Hibird, above.

It has been revealed that app: An app can make or break your smart bird feeder experience since it's where all of your bird viewing, sorting, and saving will take place. Apps with added features like useful facts, the capacity to share feeds with others, quality AI identification, and the ability to sort by bird are sometimes worth the added cost over a less-expensive feeder. Many companies use security cameras in their bird feeders that don't have a separate app—this means you'll just get a utilitarian list of image captures with no detail or context. To help buyers with their decision-making, I am at the moment building a rubric to grade and rank smart bird feeder apps, which I hope to add to this guide within the next couple of months.

How Does WIRED Test Bird Feeders?

In a recent development, I test all feeders in my rural-suburban backyard in the Pacific Northwest. I mount seed feeders on a 1-inch pole with a baffle, using the provided mounting hardware and hose clamps. If pole-mounting isn't feasible, I mount on a fence or a shepherd's hook. I hang hummingbird feeders from a shepherd's hook mounted on the side of my house. I fill the seed feeders with Audubon Wild Park bird seed and the hummingbird feeders with a nectar mixture of 4-to-1 granulated sugar and water. I keep each feeder up for a minimum of four weeks, with all app notifications enabled.

According to recent reports, I look at all app features available both with a subscription and without, seeing how often I get notifications and noting whether they are accurately picking up just birds or any type of outdoor movement, and how well the AI feature is able to distinguish bird species. I also look at connectivity, seed capacity, video quality, and how well the feeder bodies hold up to squirrels and inclement weather.

The majority of feeders I tested were provided as press samples by the manufacturer. I keep some for longer-term testing, put others in storage for future testing or comparison purposes, and donate others locally via the Buy Nothing Project.

What Do I Need to Know Before Setting Up a Smart Feeder?

Why Do Most Smart Feeders Only Run on 2.4 GHz?

This section was inspired by an email from a reader who installs home Wi-Fi systems and did not appreciate my recommending a feeder that has the option to run on 5 GHz. He's not wrong that this isn't the preferred band for a smart bird feeder, but I'll explain why someone might want 5 GHz below.

According to recent reports, first off, what is 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz? In simplest terms, these are the main radio frequency bands Wi-Fi uses to send data wirelessly between your smart bird feeder and your router. One gigahertz (GHz) is 1 billion hertz, the unit of measurement for how fast radio waves oscillate. Both bands are the accepted standards for Wi-Fi, which yes, is a name brand.

Industry observers note that it follows, then, that 2.4-GHz waves oscillate more slowly than 5-GHz waves. This also means the slower waves can travel farther and pass through walls and other obstacles more effectively. With Wi-Fi-enabled products placed outside the home, the ability to penetrate walls, trees, and other potential barriers is more vital than speed. These slower waves also result in less power consumption by devices. It makes sense that 2.4 GHz would be a preferable band for a smart bird feeder, which likely would be in or near a tree-filled area.

It has been revealed that however, 2.4 GHz is a more crowded band and thus prone to interference from other Wi-Fi networks and devices, so it can be less stable. It also results in slower overall performance, leading to sluggish downloads and lag during streaming and video calls. Most modern routers offer both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands, but some may be configured (for whatever reason) to broadcast only 5 GHz. Other routers feature something called band steering, which automatically diverts devices to the less-crowded 5 GHz. A smart bird feeder that offers dual connectivity simply provides more options. If the bird feeder is right outside your window where the router is located, you may want the faster speed. Or maybe you just don't want to try to figure out how to turn off band steering. If you're not dialed in to your router, no pun intended, it may make sense for you to consider a bird feeder with dual-band connectivity.

Recent findings suggest that as is the case with any bird feeder, squirrels love to eat at smart bird feeders, most of which are not squirrel-proof, regardless of marketing claims. However, most of the smart feeders we’ve tested are just as sturdy, if not in some cases sturdier, than analog bird feeders. The worst-case scenario is likely the squirrel eating all the seed, chewing the edges, and covering up the camera with its fuzzy butt.

It has been revealed that the yard where I test smart feeders year-round is lousy with the large and persistent rodents, and the squirrel damage I’ve sustained on test feeders has been minor. With the Birdfy Pro Duo, above, the animals chewed off the edges to better get at the seed supply when it was low, and the FeatherSnap Scout had its mounting bent. Top of mind is the 5-7-9 method of siting a bird feeder—at least 5 feet off the ground, at least 7 feet away from any structures, and at least 9 feet away from anything a squirrel could jump from (branches, fences, roofs). I explain this in more detail in my guide to keeping squirrels away from your bird feeder.

Another option is an aftermarket baffle added to feeders hanging on shepherd’s hooks, or a pole with a built-in baffle, like this one from Birdfy. Or you could use seed treated with capsaicin, or hot pepper. The taste doesn't affect birds, since they don’t have capsaicin receptors like mammals do. That noted, I’ve found capsaicin only keeps squirrels away for a couple of days, whether because they’ve gotten used to it or the pepper loses its potency when exposed to the elements. As a last resort, you could always just learn to live with the squirrels and dedicate a feeder to them, although my neighbor does this, and I'm of the mind that doing so brings even more squirrels to the area.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that around the holidays, many people like to get cosy with a cup of cocoa and a heartwarming festive movie. Personally, though, I nestle into my blanket pile and turn on the 1984 fantasy classic The NeverEnding Story. It’s a tale about a magical book, a fuzzy dragon and two heroic boys trying to save the world from a mysterious force called The Nothing that’s devouring humanity’s imagination. To fight off the fear this instills in the young protagonist, Bastian, he proclaims: “It’s not real, it’s only a story!” Well, sorry, Bastian, but I’m here to tell you that The Nothing is real, and it’s out there. Well, it may be.

In a recent development, voyager is one light day away from us. Here’s what it discovered on its epic journey.

It has been revealed that see, we think there is no place in the universe that truly has nothing in it. There are various quantum fields pervading absolutely everything, and along with them come energy and strange “virtual” particles that randomly pop in and out of existence. So, when we talk about a vacuum, we mean an area of space with the minimum possible energy, not an area with no energy at all. The vacuum of deep space, as far as we know, has the minimum possible energy.

According to recent reports, but that’s only as far as we know. There is also a chance that it is possible to have an area of lower energy – a true vacuum to our universe’s possibly false one. Were that the case, the cosmos that we know and love would be at what is called the local minimum energy, rather than the global minimum energy. To picture the difference, imagine holding an egg in a bowl. The bottom of the bowl is the local minimum – in this case, the unit is height – so it is the lowest height the egg can settle into without having energy added to overcome the barriers of the bowl’s sides. If you add that energy, say by shaking the bowl, the egg will then find its way to the global minimum height: the ground.

In a recent development, for the universe, going from a false vacuum to a true vacuum – a process called vacuum decay – would have similar consequences as the fall would for the egg. And overcoming the walls of the metaphorical bowl that safely cradles our cosmos in its false vacuum could be surprisingly, unsettlingly easy.

According to recent reports, it would begin with a bubble. Those fields that fill all of space-time obey the laws of quantum mechanics, which means that they occasionally behave in ways that are extremely unintuitive and nearly impossible to explain without a litany of equations and years of graduate school. One of those unruly behaviours is quantum tunnelling, where an extremely tiny particle can spontaneously go through a barrier, rather than over it. This would be like the egg passing straight through the bowl for no obvious reason. The likelihood of this happening to any individual particle is extraordinarily low, which is why eggs (made of many particles) never pass ghost-like through bowls. The universe has a whole lot of particles, though, so tunnelling does occasionally happen.

According to recent reports, so, say a tiny particle tunnels into a true vacuum. That would create a tiny bubble of space-time that is, at the very least, closer to truly empty than the cosmos we’re used to, or at the very most, a bubble with absolutely nothing in it, not even the quantum fields that enforce what we think of as the laws of physics. What it would be like inside that bubble and what could happen next depend on a whole lot of properties that we don’t know, such as the energy difference between the true and false vacuum and the surface tension of the membrane separating the bubble from regular space-time around it. Depending on that energy difference, the bubble could be only subtly different from the rest of the cosmos or it could be incompatible with the fundamental forces and particles that make up the universe as we know it.

That is an notable distinction because, depending on the size of the bubble and its surface tension, what happens next could be catastrophic. If the bubble is very small or has very high surface tension, it will simply shrink away and disappear just as easily as it appeared. If not, the bubble will behave just like The NeverEnding Story’s Nothing, but much, much faster (and probably without the help of a terrifying evil wolf called Gmork). It would expand outwards at the speed of light, engulfing everything it encounters. Simulations of what would happen inside the bubble universe vary in their details, but they mostly agree that the in-bubble universe would eventually collapse entirely.

Obviously, a bubble of nothing spreading throughout the universe and destroying everything in its path would be cataclysmic. The fact that we don’t even know if this is possible isn’t great, either. So, how do we tell if this could happen? It’s shockingly difficult, which is why it hasn’t been done yet. If vacuum decay is possible, the most likely mechanism for us to find out is if it were to actually happen, and because the bubble expands at the speed of light, we wouldn’t know until the moment it absorbed us. It isn’t particularly comforting news.

Does Sabrina Pasterski’s holographic theory make her the next Einstein?

Sources indicate that nevertheless, there are hints we can look for. The precise values of various constants, from the mass of the Higgs boson to the strength of the strong force, can tell us a great deal about whether each of those particles and forces are stable. If they’re all stable, great! If any of them aren’t, those are potentially liable to decay and cause a bubble of true vacuum – not great! Those measurements need to be almost unimaginably precise to know for sure, and we haven’t reached sufficient precision yet. Right now, our best measurements seem to say our universe is right on the edge of stability, and increased precision in those numbers could push us over to either side.

Industry observers note that the other hint would be to look for those very tiny bubbles of true vacuum that wouldn’t spread and devour the universe. In recent years, researchers have suggested that the area between two colliding black holes might be the perfect spot for these bubbles to pop up. That tracks with the universe not yet having been enveloped by nothingness, because the bubbles would probably immediately fall into the black holes and be safely contained before they could spread. But if there’s enough time between true vacuum foaming into existence and being swallowed up, various bubbles could merge together and form tiny black holes, which we might be able to detect as they evaporate away.

Sources indicate that my two cents is that the possibility of finding any proof of a true vacuum lies so far in the future that it’s probably best to cosy up with a nice movie and try to forget about the potential looming, unpredictable destruction of the entire universe. Can I recommend The NeverEnding Story?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets.

In a recent development, but low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris at the moment circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic.

Recent findings suggest that "In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the massive sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule.".

Recent findings suggest that as noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't.".

Each latest rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions.

In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome, with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth.

Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that rolled out on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth.

The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility.

Industry observers note that both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies. The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart.

"I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it promptly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022.

The framework was crafted by King Charles III's Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI), which drew on the expertise of academics, heads of national space agencies and experts, such as Canadian astronaut and former International Space Station commander Chris Hadfield.

"It's like Stephen Hawking remarked, 'Stop looking at your shoes and look up'," Hadfield told Space.com. "It's really easy to spend a bunch of time on the news of the day, or the news of the week, or even the news of the month, you actually need something aspirational to be able to look up to some external measure of long-term success and goodness.".

To Hadfield, the Astra Carta is an example of just that. It encourages humanity to embrace a global, peaceful outlook, which the astronaut believes will be vital to humanity's success as we venture deeper into space.

Sources indicate that "If you view the moon as an eighth continent, which essentially it is, bigger than Africa, untapped, largely unsurveyed, whose laws are we going to follow as we begin to settle there?" continued Hadfield. "Or do we just transport kind of a silly imprint of our current geopolitics?".

The Astra Carta addresses a variety of interconnected challenges over its 33 pages and the 13 Articles of its "Zero Draft", which compliments and builds on the goals of existing treaties like the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, and the U.S. Artemis Accords.

Article 8 primarily focuses on orbital debris mitigation, and encourages the use of reusable launchers and responsible satellite disposal, investing in debris removal, and boosting public knowledge of the threat through education, among other measures.

But the Astra Carta's systemic approach reaches far beyond the threat posed by space debris. The remaining 12 articles highlight a latticework of forward thinking actions, ranging from the need for greater co-ordination between satellite operators to encouraging the development of novel propulsion and life support systems.It also calls for ethical guidelines on the use of AI in space, the establishing of key performance indicators for sustainability and legal frameworks for cybersecurity while advocating for treaties that prohibit the use of automated weapons in space, and so much more.

Each topic addressed in the Astra Carta looms large enough on its own. Taken together, they appear borderline insurmountable. But the convening power of King Charles III's SMI could prove to be a powerful factor in addressing them.

Recent findings suggest that "What's interesting with the space economy is that the players within it are very fragmented, all over the world, and there isn't something that's sort of telling them what to do and how to behave in space," Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI) CEO Jennifer Jordan-Saifi told Space.com. "And so there's definitely an appetite from all of those private sector players across the world … for something to galvanise common purpose.".

To that end, the SMI has created a Space Sustainability Task Force to champion the principles of the Astra Carta, led by an advisory council that includes European Space Agency director Josef Aschbacher, UK Space Agency Director Paul Bate, Martinez and Hadfield.

The non-profit has advanced the goals of the Astra Carta at meetings of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and by working with major players, including SpaceX. It also organizes high profile events such as the Nov. 7 Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida, which honored Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman, Jeremy Hansen and Victor Glover while bringing together 450 leaders and pioneers from the space, government and business sectors.

In July earlier this year, His Majesty opened the UK Space and Defence Gateway at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus in Oxfordshire, which partnered with the SMI and created an investment council to further the principles of the framework.

Industry observers note that the Astra Carta's champions are actively engaging the private sector, governments and other luminaries. What's more, Jordan-Saifi believes that the voluntary nature of the Astra Carta could trigger widespread change faster than may be possible through the traditional U.N. system, which may need to be incorporated into country-level laws in a process that could take decades.

"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page. And then we might move to more concrete and enforceable, binding options in the future." In the meantime, Jordan-Saifi hopes that players in the space industry will play a role in holding one another accountable to observing the principles of the Astra Carta.

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain, and I don't, frankly, see the significant players taking their foot off the gas, both for commercial and for strategic reasons," explained Martinez. "But I think that there is a growing awareness of the fragility of the space domain, and so, therefore, I would expect the major actors to recognise this and to behave responsibly.".

Martinez points to SpaceX's Starlink constellation as an example of good behavior on orbit, with the firm often sharing satellite trajectories and maneuver prepares for other actors to see and plan for ahead of time. "...This is what I think we are all aspiring towards in the future, some form of global, globally coordinated, or global space traffic coordination system. which we don't yet have today.".

Industry observers note that A heightened risk comes from newcomers drawn to the growing space economy from other sectors. "They don't understand that they're entering a fragile and strategic domain, and that's where initiatives like the Astra Carta can help to socialise this awareness," continued Martinez.

But one of the greatest potential strengths of the Astra Carta may rest with its unique ability to engage the public and raise awareness in the quest for sustainability in space, as much as its capacity to galvanise the private sector.

Industry observers note that "The first step is to create social awareness of this, and I would say that one of the values of the Astra Carta is the cache of royal attention to this issue," said Martinez. "Extending the king's already well known appreciation for stewardship of the Earth environment to the orbital environment. And I think that is the real value of it … if the king is talking about this issue, [it] raises its salience and gets others to think about it.".

In this, His Majesty is supported by the SMI and a team of astronaut ambassadors, including Hadfield, U.S. astronaut Nicole Stott and ESA astronaut Tim Peake.

According to recent reports, "We're going to Antigua and Barbuda for the heads of government meeting of the Commonwealth, and the king attends that, and we're actually bringing Chris Hadfield on stage to talk to the 2.7 billion citizens of the Commonwealth about the AstraCarta," said Jordan-Saifi touting the SMI's ability to reach a vast global audience. "...We really want more and more people to be involved and be aware about space. And I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet.".

However, the sheer scope of the Astra Carta makes it a challenge to communicate to the public. Potential readers may also be surprised to find that the most up-to-date version available on the SMI website is still the "Zero Draft" — the name commonly given to unpolished works not yet ready for publication.

Jordan-Saifi assured me that the Astra Carta's Zero Draft is still relevant and accurate, but that a version 1.0 is currently going through consultation for potential release in the future.

Sources indicate that which begs the question: how would one even gauge the success of so far reaching a roadmap as the Astra Carta? Its voluntary nature makes it inherently challenging, but as Jordan-Saifi notes, there are certain metrics that could be used to indicate how far the Astra Carta has shifted the space economy towards sustainability in the future.

The SMI could track the number of countries and commercial partners that have agreed to adhere to the principles of the Astra Carta, assess public awareness and gauge the success with which its tenants have been formally adopted by the United Nations and other regulatory bodies.

Hadfield, meanwhile, reflected on the difficulties facing the Astra Carta's champions on the long road to sustainability.

"How do you weave in the role of a space agency who has to answer to the national demands and the constraints that they have, both financially and politically?" questioned the former astronaut. "And how do you weave in all of the nonprofits that have all different agendas? The Astra Carta is trying to do all those things, and I think it's done admirably, but it takes patience. And if you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake.".

Industry observers note that want to know more? Then be sure to head over to the SMI website to read the Astra Carta in full, or you can read a recent op-ed on whether we are at the moment on track for true space sustainability.

It has been revealed that anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, Latest Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

#375. How Playstation nailed its iconic startup screen

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (819 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq

How Playstation nailed its iconic startup screen

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there’s a short ritual that plays out every time someone switches on a PlayStation.
  • It has been revealed that for more than thirty years, every generation of PlayStation has opened with its own version of this sequence.
  • That intent goes back to the beginning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there’s a short ritual that plays out every time someone switches on a PlayStation. You press the power button and, before the dashboard appears, movement and sound take over, building through a sequence before the console hands you over to play. It lasts only seconds, but those seconds have a beginning, a build, a pause and a release. They are designed as an experience in their own right.

It has been revealed that for more than thirty years, every generation of PlayStation has opened with its own version of this sequence. The motion, visual language and sound have changed but the decision to design that transition has remained. What could easily be functional downtime has instead become part of the PlayStation experience. It rivals the best motion in logo design, but it also has its own function as well.

That intent goes back to the beginning. When Manabu Sakamoto designed the original PlayStation logo, he wanted it to capture one of the console’s defining promises: 3D. The interlocking P and S created a sense of depth and space rather than simply sitting flat on a 2D screen. By spring 1994, that identity had been turned into an animation, handed to sound designer Takafumi Fujisawa as what the team called a “motion logo.”.

Fujisawa was given little direction beyond that animation and had to set the tone himself, working within tight technical limits. He wanted the startup to feel like walking into a cinema. That particular hush where you sense something is about to begin.

According to recent reports, A straight cut from power-on to interface would give you a change of state and nothing else. Motion gives those few seconds structure; sound and visual design give them character. They are all working together, but motion is what determines how the experience unfolds through time.

Sources indicate that the startup’s primary job isn’t just to create an ‘atmosphere’, as it also helps organise the experience of entering the console itself. The sequence tells the player that something is happening, creates a sense of progression, and makes the eventual handoff into play feel deliberate.

On the original PlayStation, it took on a more practical role. The startup sound helped confirm that the hardware was running correctly and that the disc had been read. If it hadn’t, part of the sound was designed to loop to signal that something was wrong.

The important point is that the startup was not simply decoration sitting on top of a technical process. Motion, sound and visual design were part of how that process was communicated and felt.

That is where motion becomes especially useful. It can signal change, control pace, create anticipation and prepare someone for what comes next.

Sources indicate that over time, the original function of that startup changed. Hardware changed, interfaces changed, and the need to tell a player that a disc had been successfully read stopped mattering. Yet, PlayStation kept designing the transition.

Sources indicate that five generations on, those startups have looked, moved and sounded very different. What has survived through that time is the expectation that switching on any PlayStation from PS1 to PS5 deserves an authored beginning.

Sources indicate that that consistency does not always come from repeating the same expression. It sometimes (and in this case) comes from recognising which moments are the most valuable. PlayStation could change the way those seconds looked and felt because the thing it had established beforehand went beyond the mere execution of it.

Industry observers note that brands spend enormous amounts of time designing the things people see, whether it be the best logos, typefaces, colours, layouts or interfaces. But experiences are also full of moments between those things.

When an app opens, or a payment completes, an audience waits for something to begin. These transitions are easy to treat as functional gaps, especially when the instinct is to get people to the next thing as swiftly as possible. The point, though, is not to add friction; it is to recognise that these moments already exist, and that repeated transitions can become part of the brand experience when they are deliberately designed.

Motion matters disproportionately in those spaces because it works in the same material the moment is made of: time. It determines how one state becomes another, and how that change is experienced along the way. PlayStation was able to make that transition worth designing and returning to in its own right.

Sources indicate that andrew Vucko merges a lifelong interest in motion and design with a passion for brand building. As the founder of Vucko, he leads a global motion studio that transforms brands like Google, Meta, and Spotify through award-winning motion identities, systems, and guidelines.
