💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a latest season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).
  • Industry observers note that though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely fresh places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi.
  • An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a latest season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Industry observers note that though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely fresh places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two reveals both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Industry observers note that vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both highlights. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#291. TCL QM7L Mini-LED TV Review (2026)

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1434 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED

TCL QM7L Mini-LED TV Review (2026)

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1434 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Are we entering the era of TV “dupes”?
  • Recent findings suggest that I know this because the QM7L arrived close on the heels of a new budget OLED, the Roku Pro Series, so I was able to compare the two side by side.
  • Available in sizes ranging from 55 inches (which I tested) to a mammoth 98 inches, the QM7L boasts a virtually borderless screen that stands on a pedestal instead of the usual feet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Are we entering the era of TV “dupes”? Because to the untrained eye, or even a reasonably trained one, it’s hard to distinguish TCL’s mini-LED-powered QM7L from a lower-end OLED. So when your brother-in-law plops down in front of your new TV to watch the Lions and says, “Wow, you splurged, eh?” you can just nod and give a wink. Dupe accomplished.

Recent findings suggest that I know this because the QM7L arrived close on the heels of a new budget OLED, the Roku Pro Series, so I was able to compare the two side by side. Results: surprising. Although it has a potentially problematic design element and an AI that’s not exactly Claude-level sophisticated, the QM7L might just be the best midrange TV you can buy right now.

Available in sizes ranging from 55 inches (which I tested) to a mammoth 98 inches, the QM7L boasts a virtually borderless screen that stands on a pedestal instead of the usual feet. That’s a win if you own a small piece of furniture that might not accommodate the width of such feet, and I’d argue it’s more aesthetically pleasing too.

Industry observers note that however, it does pose a problem: Because the pedestal base sticks out in front by a little over 4 inches, it doesn’t allow a soundbar to sit snug up to the screen. You could balance it on top of the base, but that looks awkward. And because it slopes down, the soundbar doesn’t even sit level.

Sources indicate that what’s more, although the base has two height options, the taller one leaves the bottom of the TV just 2.25 inches off your TV stand. That may be enough clearance for ultra-compact soundbars like the Bose TV Speaker, but something like the Sonos Arc, which measures 3 inches high, ends up blocking a sliver of the screen.

The pedestal is also kind of a pain to assemble, with little help from the tiny diagrams in TCL’s otherwise decent setup guide. There are eight small screws used to connect the riser to the base, four more to attach it to the TV, and a bit of confusion over which of 10 mounting holes you’re meant to use.

These are hardly dealbreakers. If you’re planning to wall-mount the TV, the base becomes a non-problem. Same if you’re skipping a soundbar altogether. Or maybe you’re willing to live with it sitting out in front a few inches.

It has been revealed that setting up the TV itself is largely a breeze, especially if you already have the Google Home app on your phone. Even though I’m an iPhone guy, I was able to scan an onscreen QR code and use the app to move rapidly through the setup process. An account sign-in and Wi-Fi network selection later, I just had to wait on a software upgrade before heading to the couch.

According to recent reports, TCL’s unremarkable remote has sharp edges, the usual mishmash of Google TV buttons, and a pretty disorganized layout overall. On the plus side, it’s backlit and comes with six app-shortcut buttons.

One head-scratcher: The penultimate TV-setup screen notes that I can “customize the star button on the remote,” using it as a shortcut for this or that, which sounds great except that there is no star button.

In a recent development, speaking of hallucinations (kidding!), Google Gemini comes baked into the Google TV UI, which is reasonably easy to navigate but not without a few annoyances. For example, the top menu includes a Live TV page—home to various FAST channels, simple enough—but also a TCL page that contains … other FAST channels.

Recent findings suggest that as for Gemini, it’s nice to have but hardly essential. Just talk into the remote and you can ask for, say, movies about sharks, or learn who invented the Steadicam. The voice recognition is responsive, and the responses arrive promptly. Too bad it’s not hands-free; you have to press and hold a button on the remote to use it. Gemini also dishes up “watch now” options, and you can use it to create custom images and video clips, if you want. Unfortunately, while Gemini can accommodate basic TV commands (“Start Netflix,” “Mute the sound,” etc.), it can’t do things like open picture settings or toggling off motion-smoothing—a bummer because those commands would actually save you a little time. Instead, such requests turn into basic web searches, returning only information on how to access those settings yourself.

I was a bit disappointed with Google TV’s screensaver. It lets you draw from various sources, including an art gallery and your own photo library, but it doesn’t offer any “art mode” options like a mat overlay or automated brightness reduction. You also can’t adjust the amount of idle time before the screensaver kicks on. An art TV this is not.

Recent findings suggest that software quibbles notwithstanding, the QM7L is a joy to behold. Whatever you care to make of TCL's marketing lingo (SQD Mini-LED, the “S” stands for “Super”), the results can’t be denied: dazzling color and ocean-floor blacks that really do bring OLED to mind. In fact, I’d argue that this TV “pops” more than the aforementioned Roku OLED—not because the colors are more vibrant, but because there’s greater brightness behind them.

While watching Pixar’s Coco, for example, both TVs produced glorious hues, but my eye was more drawn to the TCL because the reds, greens, and blues just seemed to burst a bit more. (OLEDs, especially on the lower end, do tend to struggle with brightness, as detailed in my Roku Pro Series review.).

Industry observers note that even watching something like East of Eden on Netflix, with its decidedly muted color palette, it was the brightness that stood out; the QM7L revealed a bit more detail inside the Trask house. Interestingly, I also spotted a difference in the Netflix logo: On the TCL, it blazed a fire-engine red; the Roku version looked more subtle, almost orange in comparison.

It has been revealed that make no mistake, both TVs impressed me greatly. But seeing the two alongside each other, I liked the QM7L’s picture just a little better. I also watched sports and played Xbox games—both well served by the panel’s native 144-Hz refresh rate—and marveled at the smooth action and sharp lines.

Not everything was perfect, however. There were a few cases where contrast and brightness seemed a little lacking, like during an episode of the criminally underrated Halt and Catch Fire on the Roku Channel. Checking the settings, I found that the brightness had been dialed down quite a bit—but not by me.

Recent findings suggest that the prime suspect? TCL’s AI-powered “smart picture optimization,” a common bit of marketing in modern TVs. If there was any behind-the-scenes intelligence at work here, I struggled to find it. Indeed, I had to manually adjust the brightness for that show.

Even more frustrating, where was motion-smoothing management? This scourge of modern television should be off by default. With the QM7L, it arrives in full ruinous glory—and the AI isn’t smart enough to disable it in situations where it doesn’t belong: namely, everything except sports and gaming. Luckily, it’s not buried 10 menus deep; you can toggle it off pretty easily. But this is one area where Roku proved superior, its Smart Picture Max adeptly adjusting motion-smoothing for most viewing.

As for sound, the QM7L is the rare TV that doesn’t straight-up suck, thanks to tiny, down-facing speakers buried inside the cabinet. This one has two Bang & Olufsen–branded cones you can actually see, and because they’re embedded in the backside, they face backward as well. That’s not ideal for a wall-mount situation, as the audio would be forced to kind of squirt out from the sides, but the speakers do sound pretty good when the TV is freestanding. TCL doesn’t specify speaker wattage, but I can attest that they get plenty loud, and do so without distortion. However, I don’t understand why they’re positioned just a few inches apart, as the cabinet appears to have room for much more separation. Consequently, the soundstage feels pretty narrow; there’s very little “surround” to be found here. Even with this above-average audio, you’re still going to want a soundbar—hence my complaints about the pedestal stand earlier.

But if my main complaints are a wide pedestal stand and so-so AI integrations, that's good news for the QM7L. The most crucial thing, picture quality, is stunning for the price. You buy a TV for your eyes, and with this one, they're in for a treat.

#290. Breaking: Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (878 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker

Breaking: Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio.
  • To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout.
  • Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means. Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

It has been revealed that instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

Recent findings suggest that during the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

This is especially powerful for:.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Recent findings suggest that most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:.

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Recent findings suggest that customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

In a recent development, recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Recent findings suggest that create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

According to recent reports, A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

Unlike a bulky and almost always noisy treadmill, the best walking pad is a slim (ideally portable) machine that can slide under your standing desk or fit anywhere in your home. You can rack up steps while working, binge-watching reality TV, or just avoiding the looming winter. Sitting at your desk all day is literally a pain. It’s terrible for your posture and takes a toll on your physical and mental health; I know this because I'm currently typing this as a hunched-over keyboard gargoyle. Theoretically, you could take walking breaks away from your screen, but even then, you’re still spending a lot of the day on your tush.

I’m also convinced that walking pads make me more productive. Not only do you crush your daily steps before 5 pm, but daily use can boost your energy levels, mood, and cardiovascular health. Walking on an incline also strengthens and tones your lower-body muscles, so you can even get a decent workout in. There are tons on the market, offering varying speed capabilities, extra features like built-in desk platforms and wheels, and durability. Our remote testers clocked serious hours walking, working, and sometimes jogging to find the best walking pads worth the space and money.

For more WFH gear recommendations, check out Best Standing Desks, Best Laptop Stands, and Best Office Chairs.

Industry observers note that updated November 2026: I’ve added the FlexiSpot MotionX Ultra Auto Incline Walking Treadmill, Merach UltraWalk W60, and the Umay U20F Folding 3-in-1 Walking Pad. I've also added more walking pads to avoid. Product information, prices, and links were also updated.

What Features Should I Look for in a Walking Pad?

Recent findings suggest that size and storage: Walking pads are typically much smaller than traditional treadmills, but check the product dimensions and make sure the footprint will work for you. If you’re working with an especially small space, consider a foldable or under-desk walking pad. If you’re planning to store it under furniture or in a closet when not in use, shop for slimmer models with wheels for portability.

Belt size and track length: The deck size is dependent on the product’s dimensions, and you should take into consideration how much space you have to work with. But, generally, I prefer wider and lengthier belts that feel more stable to walk on, especially if you’re on the taller side or have a longer stride.

Weight capacity: Walking pads aren’t as durable as treadmills and tend to have a lower weight capacity. Check the machine’s limit, and make sure it will work for you and anyone else in the household who will be using it. Per the online reviews we’ve read, walking pads are notorious for falling apart after only a few years or even a few months of use, so it might be worth getting something that’s a little more heavy-duty.

It has been revealed that speed range: Choose a walking pad that offers a speed range that best fits your lifestyle and goals. Most models will generally offer speeds up to 4 mph, which should cover everything from gentle strolls and brisk walks, and is ideal for home office use. There are walking pad-treadmill hybrids that offer faster paces if you’re also looking for a jog.

Adjustable inclines: Some models remain flat, but I prefer the walking pads that feature adjustable levels so that you can customize your cardio intensity as you see fit. Walking at an incline can also strengthen your lower body muscles and reduce anterior knee loading.

In a recent development, metrics and display: Most walking pads have an LED display that tracks your steps, distance, time, and calories. Some models also include a remote control and/or app, which can sometimes sync your metrics from the machine, so you can check your workout data on your phone. This may not matter to you if you prefer to use your Apple Watch or fitness tracker.

Price: You can snag a solid, no-frills walking pad for under $300, but if you’re looking for a higher-end model with a surplus of features, it can cost $500+.

In a recent development, our remote team members evaluated each walking pad from their own home offices, using the pads during real workdays. Testers of different heights, stride lengths, and lifestyles walked for hour-plus stretches while answering emails, taking meetings, and performing other work-related tasks; we noted how each pad felt over time and whether any annoyances surfaced with prolonged use. We evaluated every model for at least two weeks across the following criteria:.

It weighs about 71 pounds, so moving it around isn’t fun, but the wheels help.

You can control the CyberPad (and the colorful lights along the side rails) with its Bluetooth remote and app. As long as you open the app at some point during your walk, it’ll log your workout data from the machine, so you can keep track of daily step counts over time. You can also view your current workout metrics on a screen at the front of the machine.

The speed tops out at 4 mph, and the incline stops at level nine, which can be either a 9- or 14-percent incline, depending on how you position the machine’s feet. Unfortunately, the incline capability does make it difficult to store under furniture. Here’s the full review.

This is a much longer and heavier walking pad; it’s 57 inches (32.5 inches when folded), which means it’s a good choice for taller folks or anyone who has a long stride. The deck feels stable, though not as springy or as padded as the CyberPad. You can adjust the speed via the remote control or companion app, but you don't need to set up the app to use the walking pad. You can check your time, speed, distance, calories, and steps on the large display.

Unfortunately, this machine was a bit of a pain to set up. Getting the Bluetooth remote and KS Fit app to connect was a struggle. I also don’t like that when you first start using the machine, you have to spend time walking at slower speeds before you can “unlock” the upper end of the range. The app itself is a little wonky; if you don’t start a workout with the app, your progress won’t be tracked or logged, and it doesn’t sync later. It also saves each walking session separately, so if you take a break, you start from zero again.

Sources indicate that the app also offers workouts, which auto-adjust the speed to your pace via sensors under the belt. It felt awkward, since I couldn’t figure out how to slow the pace without the device totally stopping. You switch between modes within the app or on the display, and you can stop and start the machine using the app or remote. I like to use the machine in manual mode, and I tend to use the app more than the remote, because the remote connectivity is inconsistent.

The machine feels like it will have a long lifespan. Its heft makes it harder to move around, but its foldability is a win in general. Here’s my full review. —Kristin Canning.

The Urevo Strol 2S Pro doubles as a treadmill and feels shockingly stable underfoot for how relatively lightweight it feels. It remained firmly in place even as I ran on it at top speed and incline (7.6 mph and 9 percent). That top speed isn’t fast enough if you’re looking to really sprint, but it’s definitely ample for a good workout. I really appreciated the quiet motor. Overall, it seems like a durable machine that offers great value, especially with the speed range.

If you want to use the treadmill as a walking pad, you can keep the handrail down, which limits the top speed to 4 mph (though you can still use the full incline functionality). To access faster speeds, you have to put the handrail up, which requires you to use a hex tool to tighten it into place. The handlebar has a display as well, and you can control the machine’s basic functions from there. There’s also a tablet holder you can attach.

The machine was very easy to set up, and the remote and app connected to it right away. Its companion app was my favorite of those I tested—it was intuitive, showed the info I wanted to see in my profile (like daily step counts), and synced well with the machine. There are some wonky translations, but nothing that made it hard to use. As long as you connect to your treadmill at some point during your walk (even if you start and control the machine outside the app), it will log your workout data. In the app, you can use the Quick Start function to walk freely and adjust the settings from your phone, or you can do a virtual walk with iconic scenery. —Kristin Canning.

FlexiSpot MotionX Ultra Auto Incline Walking Treadmill for $370: This walking pad offers a solid incline range, going up to a level nine, or a 12-percent incline. The 39.4-inch track felt stable underfoot, even at the highest incline and max speed (4 mph). It’s the quietest walking pad I’ve tested. You can connect your phone to play music through the speakers, too. The remote allows you to take on 30-minute, preprogrammed walking workouts, too, where the machine auto-adjusts the speed throughout (though not the incline). Otherwise, you can use it in manual mode and adjust the settings to your liking. Unfortunately, it doesn’t track step count.

It’s easy to set up, and switching between modes is quick and simple (you just need to use a small tool to adjust the rail; the tool is magnetized, so it can live on the rail and never get lost in a junk drawer). If you’re searching for a running treadmill, check out Kristin’s guide to the Best Home Treadmills.

Sperax Walking Pad: The US Consumer Product Safety Commission has warned consumers to stop using several Sperax walking pad and treadmill models due to the fall and fire hazards they pose. According to the CPSC, the machines can unexpectedly change speeds or come to a sudden stop, and there have also been reports of overheating and fires. The warning applies to the Pro, Q1, RM-01, and RM-02 models, but I’d avoid this brand altogether.

GoPlus 2-in-1 Folding Treadmill for $170: There were just too many detractors for us to recommend this budget-friendly walking pad, although we hope to test some newer versions from the same firm. And there were no on-board buttons to control the treadmill, so if you lose the remote, you'll have an expensive paperweight until you can replace it. I also found the phone holder too small and the shipping box poorly designed. While the low price is appealing, and I liked the folding handles and general feel of the belt, you’d be better off investing in one of our picks. —Louryn Strampe.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

In a recent development, despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough.".

According to recent reports, enough Phone really does seem small. The company states its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

Industry observers note that the Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

Sources indicate that as for the Enough Phone's other specs, the firm states it looks to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current strategy is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade.".

It has been revealed that now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is at the moment in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

It has been revealed that unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That remarked, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

In a recent development, of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the organization right now makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple aims to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

According to recent reports, if the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the manufacturer's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough indicates that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet.

In a recent development, NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The strategy is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth.

Recent findings suggest that the PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028.

The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples.

Industry observers note that NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars, as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself.

Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet.

NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment.

However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame.

Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion.

How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column.

Recent findings suggest that in the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? Why not let a human expedition bring back the goods?

Also speaking at MEPAG was Bruce Jakosky of the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder and Department of Earth and Space Sciences at the University of Washington.

Industry observers note that jakosky called for an integrated approach to planning human missions to Mars. He highlighted recommendations stemming from a workshop in which he participated, held last May and organized by Explore Mars, Inc.

That report focused on the impact of MSR on reducing risk for human missions, rather than focusing on the science, Jakosky told Space.com.

"The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in," remarked Jakosky. "This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear," he said.

During the MEPAG gathering, Jakosky flagged the importance of returning samples prior to human missions to Mars, such as:.

Yet one more forcing factor for NASA in yet another relook at MSR is that China is making progress on its Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission.

According to the China National Space Administration, the country's Tianwen-3 probe will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter, and an Earth reentry module.

Tianwen-3 appears on track getting the trek underway around 2028 on two Long March-5 heavy-lift carrier rockets from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China's southernmost island province of Hainan.

China's Tianwen-3 mission is dedicated to bring back to Earth roughly 500 grams of Red Planet collectibles in 2031.

#283. Breaking: Jensen Huang and the End of the Founder Fairy Tale

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (948 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED

Breaking: Jensen Huang and the End of the Founder Fairy Tale

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners.
  • What ensued was, in a word, bizarre.
  • I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was July of 2024, and Jensen Huang was punchy.

I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential manufacturer? Yes, of course. I began preparing.

What ensued was, in a word, bizarre. During the first prep call for the conference, the type of call-in which PR handlers typically try to coax specific questions out of journalists to prevent an ambush, a youngish, vaguely familiar woman took the lead. This was Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter. She was clearly intelligent, commanding respect. She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides.

Slides? Tee up Jensen? What kind of “interview” was this?

I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube.) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat.

Sources indicate that as a longtime journalist I’m used to occasional adversarial interactions; I really don’t lose sleep over them. This was just a CEO being a CEO. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Not just wanted to; he assumed he would. And to a large extent he did. Until this week.

Sources indicate that narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A parent who brought his kids into the corporate fold. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the manufacturer logo on his arm.

Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded manufacturer in history. That part’s not just fairy tale. It’s true. Now, it’s starting to read more like a Greek tragedy.

Sources indicate that back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt:.

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He stated he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories.

WIRED: It seems like an crucial part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively.

Yes. Strategy setting is storytelling. Culture building is storytelling.

You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck.

Industry observers note that that’s right. It was really about telling the story.

It has been revealed that of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China.

Sources indicate that another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once stated the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more promptly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the firm’s allocation of chips.

Industry observers note that this is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter. As one former employee put it, Huang can’t simultaneously have had knowledge of every element of Nvidia’s business and then potentially feign ignorance about where the chips may have fallen, both figuratively and literally. His apparent lapses in judgment have now led him to resign from the very company he coaxed into existence and have shattered the mythos of its ever-prescient founder.

It’s certainly not the narrative ending Huang would have chosen, were he still in control.

#281. Tech Report: Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1528 w)
Business & Policy ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily

Tech Report: Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A fossil dating back more than 450 million years has revealed something scientists almost never find: delicate soft tissues from an animal that lived hundreds of millions of years before dinosaurs appeared.
  • The fossil belongs to an ancient crinoid, a marine animal related to modern starfish.
  • Although scientists have discovered millions of crinoid fossils, nearly all preserve only hard skeletal structures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A fossil dating back more than 450 million years has revealed something scientists almost never find: delicate soft tissues from an animal that lived hundreds of millions of years before dinosaurs appeared. The extraordinarily rare discovery is giving researchers a latest understanding of how some of Earth's earliest marine animals lived, fed, and evolved.

The fossil belongs to an ancient crinoid, a marine animal related to modern starfish. Crinoids often resemble underwater flowers, with branching arms extending from a central body. More than 450 million years ago, these unusual creatures were among the animals thriving in Earth's earliest coral reefs, long before plants and animals had become widespread on land.

Although scientists have discovered millions of crinoid fossils, nearly all preserve only hard skeletal structures. Delicate body parts usually decay long before fossilization can occur, leaving major gaps in our understanding of how these ancient creatures functioned.

Now, paleontologists at the University of Oklahoma have identified an exceptionally rare specimen that preserves soft tissue structures, providing an extraordinary opportunity to investigate life in Earth's ancient oceans.

"After an animal dies, soft tissues like skin, eyes, or internal organs are the first things to decay," noted Dr. Lena Cole, OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History. "Most fossils are only made up of hard parts like bones, teeth, or shells. Soft tissues are only preserved when the environment acts almost like a natural refrigerator or vacuum‑sealer -- conditions that are incredibly rare.".

A 450 Million-Year-Old Fossil With Exceptionally Rare Soft Tissue.

It has been revealed that the remarkable specimen belongs to Dendrocrinus simcoensis, an extinct species of crinoid. Its preserved tube feet represent only the second known example of fossilized soft tissue in crinoids and the oldest such discovery ever documented.

Tube feet are small, flexible structures found in echinoderms, a group of marine animals that includes starfish, sea urchins, and crinoids. Because these structures are soft and easily destroyed after death, finding evidence of them in fossils is extraordinarily unusual.

"Preservation like this is truly one in a million," Cole added. "Crinoid fossils number in the millions, and this is only the second time soft tissues have ever been found.".

The age of the specimen makes the discovery even more remarkable. These delicate structures have been preserved in the fossil record for nearly half a billion years, offering direct evidence of anatomy that would otherwise have disappeared.

According to recent reports, "It's incredible these soft tissues have survived more than 450 million years," said Dr. David Wright, another OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, who co‑authored the study with Cole. "For reference, these soft tissues are more than 200 million years older than the oldest dinosaur.".

Ancient Feeding Structures Reveal Evolutionary Secrets.

The fossil's preserved tube feet are especially valuable because they provide clues about how crinoids obtained food and interacted with their surroundings.

Unlike the teeth and jaws that many familiar animals use to eat, crinoids rely on specialized structures to capture food particles from seawater. Their tube feet play an important role in feeding and in how these animals interact with ocean currents.

The size, arrangement, and shape of these structures can differ between species, reflecting adaptations to particular habitats and feeding methods. By studying those differences, paleontologists can reconstruct aspects of an extinct animal's lifestyle, even when no living examples of that species exist.

"Since crinoid tube feet are used for feeding, you can think of them in a similar way to how we think about teeth in mammals," Wright explained. "Differences in their structure tell us about what kinds of environments a species lived in and how it fed.".

Industry observers note that researchers also compared the ancient fossil with crinoids living in today's oceans. Those comparisons revealed notable anatomical differences, suggesting that the feeding structures of these animals have undergone substantial evolutionary changes over hundreds of millions of years.

Industry observers note that "Comparisons with living crinoids show that the anatomy of this ancient species was very different," Cole added. "This gives us newly introduced insight into how crinoids evolved and how their feeding strategies changed over hundreds of millions of years.".

A Rare Window Into Earth's Earliest Ocean Ecosystems.

Beyond revealing details about one ancient species, the discovery could help scientists piece together how marine ecosystems developed during the early Paleozoic Era.

Industry observers note that the Paleozoic was a vast chapter of Earth's history that began about 541 million years ago. During its early stages, marine environments supported an expanding variety of complex animals, while life on land was still relatively limited.

Sources indicate that crinoids were among the creatures that became established in early reef communities. Their fossils provide important evidence of how marine animals occupied different ecological roles and adapted to changing environmental conditions.

However, studying only living species cannot reveal the full range of forms and adaptations that existed in the distant past. Some extinct animals possessed anatomical features that have no close equivalent among their modern relatives.

"Fossilized remains of long‑extinct species can show features well outside the range of variation we see in living species," Wright noted.

"By comparing ecological ways of life for extinct and modern species, we can understand how patterns of adaptive evolution have changed through time and what factors shaped the modern biosphere.".

In a recent development, the biosphere includes all living organisms on Earth and the environments they inhabit. Understanding how it developed requires scientists to examine not only which species existed, but also how they interacted with their surroundings and one another.

Industry observers note that because soft tissues are so rarely preserved in ancient echinoderms, discoveries like this one provide evidence that conventional fossils cannot offer. They can help researchers identify previously unknown feeding strategies, understand ancient ecosystems, and trace evolutionary changes that eventually shaped modern marine life.

An Extraordinary Discovery Hidden in a Museum Collection.

Perhaps one of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is where the fossil was found.

Although major paleontological breakthroughs are often associated with expeditions to remote locations, valuable scientific evidence can also remain unnoticed for decades in museums.

Fossil collections contain enormous numbers of specimens, many of which have never been examined by specialists with the expertise needed to recognize their most crucial features. As scientific knowledge and research methods improve, these collections can reveal discoveries that earlier generations overlooked.

"New fossil discoveries ultimately come from fieldwork, but museum collections play a significant role in this kind of integrative research," Wright stated. "We don't always know the full significance of the specimens we collect. New technologies, ideas or expertise often find surprising ways to utilize existing specimens to make new discoveries.".

The Dendrocrinus simcoensis fossil had been housed for years at Montréal's Musée de paléontologie et de l'évolution, a small museum that operates entirely with support from community donations.

Its remarkable scientific value became apparent when Cole and Wright, both specialists in crinoids, visited the museum and examined the specimen more closely.

Their investigation revealed that the fossil preserved an extraordinarily rare record of ancient soft tissue, transforming a specimen already held in a museum collection into an important source of new evolutionary evidence.

"This discovery highlights the importance of museum collections and the community support that keeps them alive," Cole said. "Without the dedication of many people caring for these collections, this research would never have been possible.".

More Discoveries May Be Waiting in Museum Drawers.

The finding also demonstrates why preserving and maintaining fossil collections is essential for future research.

Sources indicate that at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Cole and Wright oversee invertebrate paleontology collections containing more than one million specimens. Additional fossils are added every year, creating new opportunities to investigate ancient organisms and identify previously unrecognized species.

Recent findings suggest that with collections of this size, no individual researcher could possibly examine every specimen in detail. A fossil that appears ordinary today might become the focus of a major discovery when studied by someone with a different specialty or latest scientific tools.

Making collections available to researchers around the world increases the chances that these overlooked treasures will eventually receive the attention they deserve.

"This is why we work to make our collections accessible to researchers around the world," Wright said. "There are simply too many fossils to study over one person's career. There's more than a lifetime's worth of discoveries waiting to be found.".

Sources indicate that the extraordinary crinoid fossil is a reminder that some of the most revealing clues about Earth's distant past may already have been collected. They are simply waiting for someone to recognize what makes them special.

In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A dramatic Microsoft 365 outage impacting widely used services like Outlook, Teams, and Copilot dragged into a second day on Friday after the manufacturer failed overnight to resolve an issue that left institutions and individuals around the world without crucial communication tools. The services did seem to be on a slow path to recovery by midmorning on Friday.

“We’re observing sustained improvements in service availability,” Microsoft noted in a statement posted to its status dashboard on Friday morning. The organization had said on Thursday evening that its initial attempts to fix the problem were “not taking as expected.”.

The outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies. And when they fail, the ramifications can be huge.

Microsoft has not said yet what caused the outage but has hinted that it was related to cascading server failures inside multiple data centers around the world that shifted too much load onto remaining operational machines.

“We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure,” the company wrote in Microsoft 365 Status patch on Thursday afternoon. “We’re testing a configuration change to address a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable,” the company added a few minutes later.

An additional patch a few minutes after that noted, “We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.”.

Microsoft emphasized repeatedly in statements that there was no indication of the outage being caused by a cyberattack.

Sources indicate that “This is absolutely going to go down as one of the substantial ones, up there with the Facebook outage of October 2021,” says Doug Madory, head of internet analysis at monitoring firm Infoblox. “We don't know the root cause yet, but it is interesting to break down the traffic by source data center. The recovery came in fits and starts and varied greatly by source, probably due to Microsoft's efforts to bring the service back online.”.

Recent findings suggest that A prolonged outage of such a critical underlying digital service is not unprecedented, but Microsoft has a special position among cloud providers as an older firm that was already ubiquitous in global computing from the PC era. Many organizations integrate Microsoft productivity services at the core of their operations, simply because they have used Windows computers for decades and have longstanding relationships with Microsoft.

“What makes this particularly significant is the criticality of the services affected, especially email and communication systems relied upon by government and other essential organisations,” says Swapneel Patnekar, the CEO of Indian web security firm Shreshta IT Technologies. “The impact goes well beyond the inconvenience of a typical service disruption.”.

Many observers pointed out on Thursday and Friday that Microsoft has recently shed staff through attrition, layoffs, and buyout offers. The tech giant’s annual filings say it had 223,000 full-time employees on June 30, down from 228,000 at the same time in 2025. Then in July, the company eliminated 9,000 jobs globally, of which 3,200 were cuts related to an overhaul of its Xbox teams. In October, the company reportedly made buyout offers to 60,000 employees, though apparently this was intended to speed attrition, not cull all of those roles.

Then there’s the AI factor. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella stated in April that as much as 30 percent of the code the organization is generating is now written using AI in automated tools.

“Satya's recent comments have a much different look today than they did even a week ago,” notes Jake Williams, a faculty member at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy. “I don't think we'll ever be able to say that the staff reductions caused this outage, but you'll never convince me that all the tribal knowledge that walked out the door wouldn't have been invaluable in resolving it.”.

Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Reports of widespread disruption from the Microsoft outage started appearing during the working day on Friday in countries in Asia and Australasia, spreading across the world as more people logged on.

Schools, retail stores, courts, and medical organizations across Australia said everything from exams to health care appointments were disrupted. “Medical scans have been cancelled due to both myself and the clinic not being able to access referrals via email or fax,” one person told Australian media. Officials in Japan’s government said its own platforms had been disrupted, and staff were using phones and chat tools as they couldn’t access Outlook.

According to recent reports, in the UK, multiple police forces have noted they are unable to accept online crime reports due to the outages of Microsoft services, though phone lines for emergency and nonemergency reports remained available. Parts of the National Health Service, including doctor surgeries and hospital services, also reported that some services were impacted by the outages. “Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patients in the normal way—creating a massive backlog,” the GMB trade union posted on X, referring to nonemergency and emergency health services.

Meanwhile, Deutsche Bahn, the provider of train services across Germany, updated its alerts page saying the email outages “severely restricts the sending of timetables.” Courts, local government agencies, and media organizations in the Netherlands reported concerns with their communications services, according to local press. In France, some health agencies and local governments also reported similar issues. One winemaker in South Africa told the BBC his tech giant had been brought to a standstill by the outages.

Industry observers note that unsurprisingly, these disruptions continued to be echoed across Canada and the US as millions of people have attempted to sign on. Canadian rail service Via Rail posted online that customers may not receive details of their booked trips via email, with with York’s Department of Investigation posting on X that housing evictions planned for Friday had been canceled and Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office, in Colorado, also posting on X that a lack of email notifications means bond payments being made online were not being processed.

“It's literally named 365. That implies a specific duty,” claims longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “Can’t sell an empty bottle called ‘Bottle of Water.’”.

During the outage, multiple officials around the world called for countries to rely less on giant tech firms or reevaluate their relationships. “The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services,” Chi Onwurah, the chair of the UK parliament’s Science and Technology Committee, stated in a statement.

Industry observers note that since the start of the second Trump administration—with its chaos, unpredictability, and threats changing the nature of international relationships—countries across Europe and other parts of the world have been starting to change their attitudes and reliance on some US-based big technology firms, such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services. Officials in France have been developing local, open source alternatives to Zoom, Teams, and other productivity software, while WIRED has documented dozens of other European efforts to ditch US big tech services.

Industry observers note that patnekar, from Indian security firm Shreshta, states that while much tech infrastructure has been provided by centralized services in recent years, email seems particularly challenging to create resiliency. “Ultimately, the lesson isn't necessarily that organisations should stop relying on large technology providers,” Patnekar says. “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable.”.

#277. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins.
  • Industry observers note that that said, you don’t have to keep clicking on those traffic lights over and over.
  • CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

Industry observers note that that said, you don’t have to keep clicking on those traffic lights over and over. You can simply switch to a more reputable VPN server. Moreover, browsers now offer persistent access tokens to eliminate CAPTCHA requests, while VPNs offer dedicated IPs to keep sites from getting suspicious. Here are three easy fixes for repeat CAPTCHA prompts when using a VPN, so you don’t have to trade convenience for online privacy.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

It has been revealed that most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

Sources indicate that if the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of consumers, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

According to recent reports, while there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

According to recent reports, the easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip major traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

Recent findings suggest that you should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription.

Easy to switch to a different location.

Server reputations shift over time.

Hopping between servers often can backfire.

Free intends limit server options.

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux customers. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Enabled by default on Apple devices.

Doesn't depend on your VPN or IP address.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites.

Native support for Apple devices only.

Not every site requests privacy tokens.

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable.

It has been revealed that if you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan consumers, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise aims to get one.

Sources indicate that that remarked, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation.

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs.

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work.

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription.

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers.

Locations are locked in once you pay.
